articles.title: Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation
articles.summary: Astronomers have discovered the oldest known compact pair of quasars, powered by two enormous black holes that existed just 900 million years after the Big Bang. Weighing an astonishing 1.5 billion and 400 million times the mass of the Sun, these cosmic giants somehow grew to incredible sizes far earlier than current theories can explain.
articles.content:
Astronomers have identified an extraordinary pair of quasars dating back to just 900 million years after the Big Bang. Each is powered by an enormous black hole that somehow grew to an astonishing size when the Universe was still in its infancy. Scientists have no definitive explanation for how these two cosmic giants became so massive so quickly. The remarkable pair has been given the Hawaiian name Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua.

An international research team has discovered the most distant compact pair of quasars ever observed, offering a rare glimpse into the earliest stages of cosmic history. Officially designated J1602+4228AB and nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, the pair also holds the record for the closest separation between two known quasars from the early period known as cosmic dawn.

Although astronomers believe paired quasars should be relatively common, finding and studying them is exceptionally difficult. Discovering two so close together, especially from such an early period in the Universe's history, makes this finding particularly remarkable.

The discovery was made possible by combining observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Gemini North telescope on Maunakea, a dormant volcano in Hawai'i. The research was led by Silvia Onorato, a postdoctoral research associate at NSF NOIRLab, and is described in a paper published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Gemini North is one of the two telescopes that make up the International Gemini Observatory. Operated by NSF NOIRLab, the observatory is an international partnership led by the U.S. National Science Foundation, with participation from Canada, Chile, Brazil, Argentina, and the Republic of Korea.

How Giant Black Holes Formed in the Early Universe

During the first billion years after the Big Bang, the Universe underwent a period of extraordinary transformation. Vast concentrations of invisible matter, known as dark matter halos, collapsed under gravity. The earliest galaxies began producing stars, while increasingly massive galaxies developed the first supermassive black holes at their centers.

As galaxies passed near one another, collided, and sometimes merged, enormous quantities of gas and stars became available to feed their central black holes. Some of the material falling toward these black holes released tremendous amounts of energy. This process, known as accretion, could generate radiation so intense that the glowing region surrounding a black hole outshone every star in its host galaxy.

Astronomers call these extraordinarily luminous objects quasars.

Because galaxy encounters and mergers occur frequently throughout the Universe, researchers expect many quasars to exist in pairs separated by distances smaller than the typical diameter of a galaxy. Yet detecting these systems has remained a major challenge.

One reason is that a supermassive black hole spends only a relatively brief period in its bright "quasar phase." Another is the enormous distance separating ancient quasars from Earth, which makes them appear extremely faint to ground-based telescopes. Even when both objects are visible, their close proximity can make it difficult to distinguish one from the other.

Two Monster Black Holes That Grew Too Big, Too Fast

Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua stands out because it is only the third known quasar pair from cosmic dawn. More importantly, its two black holes were already so enormous at such an early stage of cosmic history that existing theories cannot definitively explain their growth.

The black holes are separated by approximately 18,100 light-years, equivalent to about one-fifth the diameter of the Milky Way. One has an estimated mass of 1.5 billion Suns, while the other weighs approximately 400 million solar masses.

Astronomers see the pair as it appeared only 900 million years after the Big Bang, when the Universe was still populated by relatively young stars, galaxies, and black holes. Finding two black holes comparable in mass to many present-day supermassive black holes at this early time raises difficult questions about how quickly the first enormous cosmic structures could assemble.

"There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our Universe, much less two," says Onorato. "We observed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua at a time when the Universe was only a thirteenth of its age and astonishingly, its supermassive black holes are just as massive as those we see today."

The pair's Hawaiian name reflects the extraordinary forces involved. Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua translates to "Two celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness in the brilliance of heat reincarnating energy into the Universe."

The name was developed through the A Hua He Inoa program, a collaboration involving the ʻImiloa Astronomy Center of Hawaiʻi and the University of Hawai'i's Ka Haka ʻUla O Keʻelikōlani (Hawaiian Language College).[1]

How James Webb and Gemini North Revealed the Hidden Pair

The discovery began with data collected by the Aether survey, a JWST research program designed to identify and characterize objects from the early Universe. The project is led by Emanuele Paolo Farina, an Associate Scientist at NSF NOIRLab/Gemini.

Using JWST's Near-Infrared Spectrograph Integral Field Unit, the survey assembled observations of 200 quasars. That sample represents approximately 43% of all quasars known from this period of cosmic history.

While visually examining the survey data, researchers noticed something unexpected. A previously identified quasar, J1602+4228A, appeared to have a companion.

To investigate, the team turned to Gemini North's Gemini Near-Infrared Spectrograph (GNIRS). These observations allowed astronomers to distinguish the two quasars individually, providing crucial evidence about the nature of the system.

Obtaining those measurements was an exceptional achievement. The objects are separated by such a small apparent distance, and the companion J1602+4228B is so faint, that resolving them with a telescope on Earth was expected to be nearly impossible.

Fortunately, the researchers benefited from exceptionally favorable observing conditions on Maunakea. Clear skies and unusually sharp atmospheric conditions enabled them to gather the necessary observations in just two nights.

"The sky over Maunakea was so clean and sharp that we managed to collect the data in only two nights," says Onorato.

The team also used Gemini North's Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS) to gather additional information about the system and refine their understanding of the two quasars.[2]

A New Clue to the Universe's First Giant Galaxies

Exactly how Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua formed remains unknown. However, the researchers believe its extraordinary properties could point to an unusually dense concentration of matter in the early Universe.

In such an environment, frequent interactions between young galaxies may have provided enormous supplies of gas, simultaneously accelerating the birth of stars and fueling rapid growth of the black holes at their centers.

If this interpretation is correct, the quasar pair could help scientists understand how the earliest massive galaxies developed alongside their central supermassive black holes.

"Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is a really unique environment," says Onorato. "It's a laboratory for astronomers to study how the very first massive galaxies and their central black holes assembled together through direct galaxy interactions during these early times."

Notes

articles.title: A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way
articles.summary: A surprising discovery suggests the Milky Way may be making stars in places where most galaxies cannot. Scientists found evidence that a massive rotating structure near the galactic center is creating powerful shock waves that trigger star formation rather than suppress it. Even more unexpectedly, part of the Norma spiral arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a vast region where new stars are being born.
articles.content:
New research suggests the Milky Way produces stars in an unexpected location, revealing a surprising difference between our galaxy and most of its neighbors. The findings also raise questions about a familiar feature of the Milky Way, suggesting that part of what astronomers have long considered a spiral arm may actually be something else.

The discovery comes from research led by a University of Sydney PhD student, who found evidence that a massive rotating structure of stars near the galactic center is generating powerful shock waves through surrounding clouds of gas. These waves squeeze the gas together, creating conditions that allow new stars to form in a region where such intense forces usually prevent their birth.

Published in Nature Astronomy, the study also casts doubt on the nature of the Norma spiral arm, a feature of the Milky Way named for the constellation Norma as seen from Earth.

Lead author Dr. Hillary Davis, who recently completed her PhD at the University of Sydney's School of Physics and Sydney Institute for Astronomy, said the research provides new insights into the structures near the galactic center and how gas moves around them.

"At its heart, star formation is a process we understand from everyday physics. Forces set matter in motion. In this case gas is compressed, and that compression can create the conditions for new stars to be born on a massive scale," Dr. Davis said.

"In most similar galaxies, star formation very commonly occurs along spiral arms. What's extraordinary is seeing this happen in a different region of our Galaxy, where shocks are usually so strong that star formation is often suppressed."

A Hidden Star Factory at the Heart of the Milky Way

The Milky Way belongs to a class of galaxies known as barred spiral galaxies. Unlike galaxies with only a central concentration of stars and surrounding spiral arms, these systems contain an elongated structure of stars stretching across their central region. In our galaxy, this structure is called the Galactic bar.

As the bar rotates, its gravity influences nearby gas, driving it into powerful shock fronts. These fronts compress the gas in much the same way that a shock wave compresses air.

Studying this structure from Earth is particularly difficult because we are located inside the Milky Way rather than viewing it from the outside. Large amounts of cosmic dust also block our view of the galactic center.

"The Galactic bar cannot be easily observed because of a combination of our position in the Galaxy and dust obscuring our view," Dr. Davis said.

"As a result, the bar's properties have been highly debated."

Observations of other barred galaxies have shown that these shock fronts generally inhibit the formation of new stars, even in regions containing abundant gas. The intense conditions make it difficult for the gas to collapse into stars.

However, the new findings indicate that the Milky Way may behave differently. Although it is not the only known example, our galaxy appears to belong to a relatively small group in which substantial star formation takes place along the shock fronts of the central bar.

"We believe that the Milky Way's bar has star formation occurring along its shock front, which is uncommon for most bars in nearby galaxies," Dr. Davis said.

A Milky Way Spiral Arm May Not Be What It Seems

To investigate this unusual activity, the research team compared detailed computer simulations showing how galaxies change over billions of years with astronomical observations of regions where massive stars are forming.

A crucial part of the evidence came from masers, naturally occurring sources that emit highly concentrated microwave radiation. These emissions are associated with the formation of massive stars and operate on a principle similar to lasers, but at microwave wavelengths.

By examining the positions of these masers, the researchers uncovered a striking match between actual observations and the locations of shock fronts predicted by their simulations.

"We found that masers previously associated with the Norma arm closely align with the shock front predicted by our simulations," Dr. Davis said. "This suggests that at least part of the so-called Norma arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a region of star formation along the leading edge of the Galactic bar.

"This raises questions about the Galaxy's spiral structure, and the bar region of the Milky Way, which needs further investigation," she said.

The possibility is significant because it suggests that some of the star formation previously attributed to the Norma spiral arm could instead be occurring along the central bar. If confirmed, this interpretation would change how astronomers understand the arrangement of stars and gas in that part of the Milky Way.

New Evidence Could Redraw the Milky Way's Map

Beyond revealing an unusual location for star birth, the research also sheds light on the physical properties of the Galactic bar itself.

Astronomers have debated the structure's length, orientation, and rotation speed for decades, partly because the Milky Way's dust and our viewing position make direct measurements so challenging.

"Our findings place further constraints on the size, angle and rotation speed of this central bar," Dr. Davis said.

The team's analysis indicates that the bar extends approximately 4.3 kiloparsecs, equivalent to about 14,000 light-years, outward from the galactic center along its long axis. This supports a picture of the Milky Way containing a relatively long bar that rotates slowly.

The results illustrate how increasingly sophisticated simulations can help scientists investigate regions of our galaxy that are difficult to observe directly. By comparing models spanning billions of years with the available astronomical evidence, researchers can narrow down the possible structures and processes shaping the Milky Way.

"By comparing a new generation of large-scale computerized galaxy simulations, evolving over billions of years, against a more limited set of observations, we now have a stronger understanding of the bar and star formation processes in the Milky Way," Dr. Davis said.

The authors reported no competing interests. Research funding came from the Australian Research Council, the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation, the Swedish Research Council, the Swedish National Space Agency, the LMK Foundation and eSSENCE (Sweden).

Computing resources and data storage were provided through National Computing Infrastructure Australia, an NCRIS capability supported by the Australian Government, and LUNARC, the Centre for Scientific and Technical Computing at Lund University, Sweden.

articles.personality_title: New discovery reveals unusual star formation near Milky Way’s center
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context**  
The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy, meaning it has a central bar-shaped group of stars and spiral arms extending outward. Usually, new stars form along these spiral arms. Scientists have long studied the galaxy’s structure but face challenges because we observe it from inside, and dust blocks our view of the center.

**What happened**  
A research team led by Dr. Hillary Davis from the University of Sydney found that the Milky Way is forming stars in a surprising place: along shock waves created by the galaxy’s central bar. These shock waves compress gas clouds near the center, triggering star birth in an area where star formation is usually rare. The team also discovered that part of what was thought to be the Norma spiral arm might actually be a region of star formation along the bar, not a spiral arm.

**Impact**  
This discovery changes how scientists understand the Milky Way’s structure and star formation. It shows that, unlike most similar galaxies where shock waves stop stars from forming, our galaxy’s bar actually helps create them. The finding also suggests the map of our galaxy needs updating because the Norma arm may not be a true spiral arm but part of the star-forming bar region.

**What's next step**  
Further studies will focus on confirming the new interpretation of the Norma arm and exploring the Milky Way’s bar in more detail. Improved simulations and observations will help refine the galaxy’s map and deepen understanding of how star formation works in these unusual conditions.

**One-sentence takeaway**  
Scientists have found that the Milky Way’s central bar creates shock waves that trigger star formation, revealing new details about our galaxy’s structure and how stars are born in unexpected places.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle découverte révèle une formation d’étoiles inhabituelle près du centre de la Voie lactée
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte**  
La Voie lactée est une galaxie spirale barrée, ce qui signifie qu’elle possède une barre centrale d’étoiles entourée de bras spiraux. Habituellement, les nouvelles étoiles se forment le long de ces bras spiraux. Les scientifiques étudient depuis longtemps la structure de la galaxie, mais observent depuis l’intérieur, ce qui complique la vision à cause de la poussière qui cache le centre.

**Ce qui s’est passé**  
Une équipe de recherche dirigée par le Dr Hillary Davis de l’Université de Sydney a découvert que la Voie lactée forme des étoiles dans un endroit surprenant : le long d’ondes de choc créées par la barre centrale de la galaxie. Ces ondes compriment les nuages de gaz proches du centre, déclenchant la naissance d’étoiles là où elle est normalement rare. L’équipe a aussi trouvé qu’une partie du bras spiral Norma pourrait en réalité être une région de formation d’étoiles liée à la barre, et non un vrai bras spiral.

**Impact**  
Cette découverte change la compréhension de la structure de la Voie lactée et de la formation d’étoiles. Elle montre que, contrairement à d’autres galaxies similaires où les ondes de choc empêchent la formation d’étoiles, la barre de notre galaxie favorise leur création. Cela suggère aussi qu’il faut revoir la carte de notre galaxie car le bras Norma pourrait ne pas être un vrai bras spiral mais une partie de la région de formation d’étoiles.

**Prochaine étape**  
Les prochaines recherches viseront à confirmer cette nouvelle interprétation du bras Norma et à étudier plus en détail la barre centrale. Des simulations améliorées et des observations plus précises permettront de mieux comprendre la carte de la galaxie et la formation d’étoiles dans ces conditions particulières.

**Résumé en une phrase**  
Des scientifiques ont découvert que la barre centrale de la Voie lactée crée des ondes de choc qui déclenchent la formation d’étoiles, révélant de nouveaux détails sur la structure de notre galaxie et la naissance des étoiles dans des endroits inattendus.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo descubrimiento revela formación estelar inusual cerca del centro de la Vía Láctea
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto**  
La Vía Láctea es una galaxia espiral barrada, lo que significa que tiene una barra central de estrellas con brazos espirales a su alrededor. Normalmente, las nuevas estrellas se forman en esos brazos espirales. Los científicos han estudiado mucho la estructura de la galaxia, pero la observan desde dentro y el polvo bloquea la vista del centro.

**Qué pasó**  
Un equipo de investigación liderado por la Dra. Hillary Davis de la Universidad de Sídney descubrió que la Vía Láctea está formando estrellas en un lugar inesperado: a lo largo de ondas de choque creadas por la barra central de la galaxia. Estas ondas comprimen las nubes de gas cerca del centro, lo que provoca el nacimiento de estrellas en una zona donde normalmente es raro. También encontraron que parte del brazo espiral Norma podría no ser un brazo real, sino una región de formación estelar ligada a la barra.

**Impacto**  
Este descubrimiento cambia la forma en que los científicos entienden la estructura y la formación estelar de la Vía Láctea. Muestra que, a diferencia de galaxias similares donde las ondas de choque impiden la formación de estrellas, la barra de nuestra galaxia ayuda a crearlas. También sugiere que el mapa de nuestra galaxia necesita ser actualizado porque el brazo Norma podría ser parte de la región de formación estelar de la barra y no un brazo espiral verdadero.

**Próximo paso**  
Las próximas investigaciones buscarán confirmar esta nueva idea sobre el brazo Norma y estudiar la barra central con más detalle. Simulaciones mejoradas y observaciones ayudarán a perfeccionar el mapa de la galaxia y a entender mejor cómo se forman las estrellas en estas condiciones especiales.

**Resumen en una frase**  
Los científicos han descubierto que la barra central de la Vía Láctea crea ondas de choque que provocan la formación de estrellas, revelando nuevos detalles sobre la estructura de nuestra galaxia y el nacimiento de estrellas en lugares inesperados.

articles.title: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded
articles.summary: Massive stars may be quietly collapsing into black holes without ever producing the spectacular supernova explosions scientists typically expect. A surprising pattern in 257 black hole mergers suggests these mysterious stellar disappearances could explain the origins of a large population of black holes throughout the universe.
articles.content:
The biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space. Their remaining cores collapse under gravity, forming neutron stars or, in some cases, black holes. But scientists have long suspected that some massive stars meet a very different fate. Instead of exploding, they may collapse directly into neutron stars or black holes, effectively disappearing without a bang.

New research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes. Using gravitational wave observations from the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA detector network, researchers identified patterns suggesting that a distinct population of black holes could have formed from stars that never went supernova. Although the findings do not directly confirm the existence of these failed supernovae, they closely match theoretical predictions about how such black holes should be distributed.

The discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy. LIGO, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory, is funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and operates detectors in Louisiana and Washington. In 2015, the observatory made history by directly detecting gravitational waves for the first time. These tiny disturbances in spacetime were generated by two black holes colliding. Since then, LIGO has teamed up with the Virgo observatory in Italy and the Kamioka Gravitational-wave Detector (KAGRA) in Japan. Together, the network has recorded more than 300 black hole collisions.

A Hidden Population of Black Holes

"A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our Sun," says LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, a Caltech physics professor and William H. Hurt Scholar. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin -- they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova. These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract."

Chatziioannou led the study, which was published in Physical Review D. The lead author, Isaac Legred (PhD '25), is now a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and completed the work while at Caltech. Jacob Golomb (PhD '25), a former member of Chatziioannou's research group who now works at Asari AI, also contributed to the research.

Despite decades of investigation, astronomers have yet to confirm a specific case of a failed supernova. The theory, however, has a strong scientific foundation. Researchers have proposed that many merging black holes weighing approximately 10 times as much as the Sun may have originated from stars that collapsed without exploding. In these mergers, either the heavier black hole or both black holes could have formed through this process. The Caltech team set out to determine whether existing gravitational wave observations supported that possibility.

A Mysterious Gap in Black Hole Masses

To investigate, the scientists examined the masses of black holes involved in 257 mergers detected by the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA network during the past decade. A striking pattern emerged. Black holes weighing roughly 10 times the mass of the Sun were exceptionally common, appearing in about three-quarters of the merger sample.

Even more surprisingly, the researchers identified a noticeable shortage of black holes weighing between 12 and 16 solar masses. This was the first time such a distinct gap had been found in the mass distribution, raising new questions about what determines the sizes of black holes when they form.

"We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," Legred says. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes."

The researchers also examined how quickly the black holes rotate, since their spin rates can preserve clues about the conditions under which they formed. They found that black holes near 10 solar masses tended to have spin rates concentrated within a smaller range than those of the broader black hole population (the spins are also influenced by how the black holes formed).

Taken together, the unusual concentration of black hole masses, the scarcity of objects in the 12 to 16 solar mass range, and the similarities in their rotation suggest that these black holes may belong to a distinct population with a shared formation history. One possible explanation is that many originated when massive stars collapsed directly into black holes without producing supernova explosions.

Gravitational Waves Offer Clues to Silent Stellar Deaths

Finding stars that disappear without exploding presents a major challenge for astronomers. Ordinary supernovae produce brilliant flashes that can be detected across enormous cosmic distances. Failed supernovae, by contrast, may leave little visible evidence of what happened, making it difficult to identify them through conventional observations.

"We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred says. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed. Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting."

By studying the gravitational waves released when black holes merge, scientists can investigate the origins of objects whose formation may have produced little or no visible explosion. The new findings provide another piece of evidence that massive stars can follow different paths at the ends of their lives, potentially revealing how a substantial fraction of the universe's black holes came into existence.

The research, titled "Low-mass failed supernovae and the 10 solar-mass peak in the merging black hole mass distribution," received funding from the National Science Foundation, the U.S. Department of Energy, and the Simons Foundation. LIGO is operated by Caltech and MIT.

articles.personality_title: Scientists find signs of black holes formed by stars that quietly collapse

This pattern suggests some black holes formed from stars that collapsed quietly, without a supernova.

articles.title: Mysterious Mercury gets a visitor - after spacecraft's eight-year epic voyage
articles.summary: The mission is set to give us our best ever view of Mercury - the closest planet to the Sun.
articles.content:
After an eight-year journey travelling almost six billion miles (10bn km), a spacecraft called BepiColombo has arrived at its final destination and is now in orbit around Mercury.

It‘s operating in an extremely hostile environment: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and temperatures can reach a fierce 430C and then plunge to -180C, and it is constantly blasted with intense solar radiation.

Until now, the planet has been little explored but the hope is this mission will solve some of Mercury's major mysteries.

These include uncovering why there is ice in its craters despite its proximity to the Sun, and understanding the mysterious hollows that are dotted all over its surface.

"I think it's a little bit of an under-loved planet in the inner Solar System, but I think that's one of the reasons why it is so compelling," said Prof Emma Bunce, from Leicester University, who is a principal investigator on the mission.

"There are lots of reasons, scientifically, why we really want to understand Mercury, how it formed, how it evolved, what it looks like today, but also how it interacts with the Sun and the extreme space weather that it experiences."
articles.reasoning: The article reports the successful arrival of the BepiColombo spacecraft at Mercury after an eight-year journey, marking a significant milestone in space exploration. This mission promises to provide unprecedented scientific insights about Mercury, a largely unexplored planet, which can enhance our understanding of planetary formation, evolution, and solar interactions. The story is focused, detailed, and highlights a major scientific achievement with broad significance for humanity's knowledge of the solar system.
articles.personality_title: Spacecraft arrives at Mercury after eight-year journey to study the planet up close
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and has been hard to study because of its extreme temperatures and intense solar radiation. Until now, we have only had limited information about this mysterious planet.

**What happened** – The spacecraft BepiColombo completed an eight-year trip covering almost six billion miles and has now entered orbit around Mercury. It will start taking detailed measurements and pictures to learn more about the planet.

**Impact** – This mission is important because it will help scientists understand why Mercury has ice in its craters despite being so close to the Sun. It will also investigate strange features called hollows on its surface. These discoveries can teach us about how Mercury formed and how it reacts to the Sun’s powerful energy.

**What’s next step** – BepiColombo will continue to orbit Mercury, sending back data for scientists to study. Over time, this information will reveal new facts about Mercury’s environment and history, which have been mostly unknown until now.

**One-sentence takeaway** – After a long journey, the BepiColombo spacecraft is now orbiting Mercury to uncover the planet’s hidden secrets and improve our understanding of the solar system.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une sonde arrive sur Mercure après un voyage de huit ans pour étudier la planète de près

**Ce qui s’est passé** – La sonde BepiColombo a terminé un voyage de huit ans couvrant presque six milliards de miles et est maintenant en orbite autour de Mercure. Elle va commencer à prendre des mesures détaillées et des images pour en apprendre plus sur la planète.

**Impact** – Cette mission est importante car elle aidera les scientifiques à comprendre pourquoi Mercure possède de la glace dans ses cratères malgré sa proximité avec le Soleil. Elle étudiera aussi des formations étranges appelées « creux » à sa surface. Ces découvertes peuvent nous apprendre comment Mercure s’est formée et comment elle réagit à l’énergie puissante du Soleil.

**Prochaine étape** – BepiColombo continuera à orbiter Mercure en envoyant des données aux scientifiques. Au fil du temps, ces informations révéleront de nouveaux faits sur l’environnement et l’histoire de Mercure, encore largement inconnus.

**Phrase clé** – Après un long voyage, la sonde BepiColombo est maintenant en orbite autour de Mercure pour découvrir les secrets cachés de la planète et améliorer notre compréhension du système solaire.

articles.personality_presentation_es:
